title: How to Clean or Replace a Faucet Aerator: Debris Removal and Flow Restoration (This Old House)
summary: This Old House walkthrough explains faucet aerators, including how a built-in flow restrictor governs water through a small orifice and how debris can clog the path. The presenter demonstrates safe removal with a non-damaging wrench on an aerator with straight edges, reveals debris (notably coffee grounds) inside, flushes the spout to verify cleanliness, and decides that replacement may be more cost-effective than thorough cleaning. The segment concludes with a quick hot/cold water test to confirm restored flow and function, noting a rough replacement cost in the five to six dollar range.

sections.description: The video explains the aerator’s original role in shaping the stream and, with water conservation, the presence of a flow restrictor that forces water through a small hole. The narrator notes that debris or foreign matter between the aerator and the flow restrictor can prevent proper flow, explaining why blockage can shut off water pressure.

sections.title: Decision to replace the aerator after debris observation
sections.description: After observing significant debris, the presenter suggests replacing the entire aerator rather than attempting a cleaning. A rough cost estimate is discussed, signaling a practical trade-off between time and expense.

sections.title: Post-replacement testing: hot and cold flow
sections.description: The final portion demonstrates testing the faucet after replacement to confirm that hot and cold water flow are restored and functioning as expected.
